standard.title: Development of an Asian Society in Relation to the World by 1914
standard.description: the development of an Asian society in relation to other nations in the world by 1914, including the influence of nationalism and self-determination
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the full arc of the selected Asian society's history in Year 9 — its features before European contact, the effects of colonisation, key events and figures, continuities and changes around 1900, and the perspectives of colonisers and colonised. This descriptor is the capstone of the Asian history depth study, asking students to situate the selected society in relation to the world by 1914 and evaluate the influence of nationalism and self-determination.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the development of the selected Asian society in relation to other nations in the world by 1914, including the influence of nationalism and self-determination.

nodes.label: The selected society's position in the world and confrontation with Western powers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the confrontation between the selected Asian society and Western powers and explain how this shaped the society's position in relation to other nations by 1914.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the position of the selected Asian society in relation to major world powers by 1914, including one key confrontation or point of tension with Western powers.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the confrontation between the selected Asian society and Western powers — for China: the Sino-French War, the effects of the Boxer Rebellion and subsequent Protocol, and China's weakened position by 1914; for Japan: the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) as a turning point demonstrating Asian military power over a European nation; for India: the growing independence movement and confrontation with British authority; for Indonesia: the emerging nationalist movements against Dutch colonial rule — explaining how each society's relationship to Western power had been shaped by the full period of contact.
wider: Examine the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) as a global turning point — investigating how Japan's victory over Russia was interpreted across colonised Asia and Europe, and assess why it mattered beyond the two nations directly involved

Compare two Asian societies' positions in the world by 1914 — one that had successfully modernised (Japan) and one that remained under heavy colonial pressure (India) — to examine how different responses to Western imperialism produced different outcomes

Investigate how the independence movements developing in Asian societies by 1914 connected to the global spread of nationalist ideas — tracing how ideas about self-determination moved through colonial networks
nodes.hinge_reason: Situating the selected society in relation to the world by 1914 is the integrating task for the entire depth study — it requires students to bring together their understanding of the society's history from K19 to K23. Without this synthesis capacity, students will describe events without being able to evaluate their cumulative significance.

response_modes.reason: The comparative and evaluative demands of this descriptor — where does the selected society stand in relation to other nations, and why? — require explicit scaffolding. Students who lack a framework for international comparison will default to description.

success_criteria: Explains the position of the selected Asian society in relation to major world powers by 1914, with reference to specific events or conditions
Describes at least one confrontation or point of tension between the selected society and Western powers, explaining its significance

nodes.label: Nationalism and self-determination in the selected society by 1914
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of nationalist ideas and self-determination movements on the development of the selected Asian society in relation to the world by 1914.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how nationalist ideas influenced the development of the selected Asian society by 1914, with one specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the effects of nationalist ideas and self-determination on the selected society's development — for China: the revolutionary nationalism of Sun Yat-sen and the 1911 Revolution that ended the Qing dynasty; for Japan: the expression of Japanese nationalist identity through Meiji modernisation and imperial expansion; for India: the Indian National Congress's growing demand for self-governance and the political writings of figures such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Bal Gangadhar Tilak; for Indonesia: the emergence of Budi Utomo (1908) and Sarekat Islam as nationalist organisations.
wider: Examine how Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People (nationalism, democracy, people's livelihood) drew on both Chinese tradition and Western political philosophy — assessing how anti-colonial nationalism was not simply a rejection of Western ideas but a creative synthesis

Investigate how the Indian National Congress by 1914 contained both moderate and more assertive nationalist positions — examining the debate between Gokhale's constitutionalist approach and Tilak's more confrontational stance as evidence of how nationalist movements contain internal diversity

Examine how the Meiji Restoration expressed Japanese nationalism not as anti-colonial resistance but as competitive modernisation — assessing how Japan navigated the threat of colonisation by adopting some features of the colonising powers

response_modes.reason: This node is the capstone of the depth study — integrating the full arc of events, effects, perspectives, and now nationalist responses into an evaluation of the society's position by 1914. It connects to the S-strand skills of historical argument and evaluation.

success_criteria: Explains how nationalist ideas influenced the development of the selected Asian society by 1914, with reference to at least one specific movement, organisation, or figure
Assesses how the selected society's development in relation to other nations by 1914 reflected the cumulative impact of European contact and internal nationalist responses
